newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's populist Reform leader forms opposition.
newsitem.headline: Canada's populist Reform leader forms opposition.

text.p: When Canadians voted to make the right-wing Reform party and its populist leader Preston Manning the official opposition, they exposed the regional strife in the nation's politics, analysts said on Tuesday.

"We haven't had a regionalized government like this for a long time," political analyst Fred Fletcher said after the 54-year-old Manning propelled his Western-based party to the official opposition spot just 10 years after he created it.

With 60 seats in the House of Commons, up from 52, Reform will act as the government in waiting, forming a shadow cabinet to keep watch on the Liberals who won a slim second majority government on Monday with 155 out of 301 seats.
Reform replaces the separatist Bloc Quebecois as official opposition, putting an end to the quirk of having an official opposition that wants to break up the country.

"We've come a long, long way," Manning said at his victory party in Calgary. But the victory is bittersweet. His party has become increasingly regional, with support coming mainly from the Western provinces of Alberta and British Columbia.

He failed to make inroads into Ontario, Canada's richest and most populous province, losing even the single seat Reform had held there during the last parliament. He has no presence anywhere east of the Manitoba border.

"We wanted a breakthrough in Ontario," Manning lamented. But he added: "The West believes it has the answer to national problems. The West is a region whose opinions simply cannot be denied by central Canada or Ottawa any longer."

With the Reform party representing the West, the ruling Liberals deriving their support mainly from Ontario, the Bloc Quebecois strong in Quebec and the Conservatives showing strength in the Atlantic provinces, the next parliament will be plagued with regional tensions, said Fletcher, a professor of political science at York University.

As Canada prepares for another referendum on Quebec independence, regional rivalry and how the West treats Quebec will likely be key issues. Manning has vowed to push his no-nonsense approach to Quebec while also promoting smaller government, tax cuts, a crackdown on crime and more government accountability.
"This is the season of transition and it's one to be welcomed rather than be feared," he said.
Still, opponents are wary of him.
"He taps into the emotional, angry part of the voter who is frustrated," said Jan Brown, a former Reform member of parliament who fell out with the party. "It's all hot-button politics."
Manning, a religious family man and history buff who has spent most of his career challenging political orthodoxy, has run up against accusations of intolerance and racism.

Quebec Premier Lucien Bouchard said it would be "disaster" for Canada if Manning became opposition leader. Alexa McDonough, the leader of the leftist New Democratic Party, accused him of moving the country toward "civil war".
Reform television advertisements that questioned the ability of Quebec-born politicians to keep Canada united inflamed tempers in Quebec, prompting accusations of racism and intolerance.

Conservative leader Jean Charest, a Quebecker, labeled Manning a "bigot" last week, calling him "anti-Quebec, anti-francophone." But for many, Manning simply voices their concerns, saying things out loud that other political leaders dare not utter.
